offence_severity: Minimum 6 months, maximum 2 years of imprisonment and fine
financial_property_loss: Rs 7,50,000 towards completed work and Rs 1,00,000 towards caution deposit
key_evidence_accepted: The complaint contained sufficient description of the nature of the partnership, the business being carried on, the role of each accused in the conduct of the business, and the specific role of each in relation to the transactions leading to the dishonour of cheques.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the complainant's averments as sufficient to meet the requirements of Section 141(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, and considered the accused's assurances and conduct as part of the evidence.

trial_duration.supreme_court_decision: Allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment

legal_representation.accused: Abhimanyu Bhandari, Ms. Akriti Chaubey, Ms. Roohina Dua, Kunwar Aditya Singh, Ejaz Maqbool, S. Udaya Kumar Sagar, Mrityunjai Singh
legal_representation.state: Ms. Bhabhna Das, Krishna Dev Jagarlamudi

investigation_status: Complaint filed under s.138 NI Act, High Court quashed the complaint, Supreme Court allowed the appeal

appeal_history.supreme_court: Allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the complaint contained sufficient averments to meet the requirements of Section 141(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, and that the High Court was in error in quashing the complaint against the first respondent.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the High Court was correct in quashing the complaint as there was no averment that the first respondent was in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of the business, and that the first respondent had no day-to-day connection with the partnership firm.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that a partnership firm is included within the definition of 'company' under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, and that the complaint must be read holistically to determine if it meets the requirements of Section 141(1).
precedent_relied_upon: Gunmala Sales Private Limited v. Anu Mehta and Others (2015) 1 SCC 103
